q: A channel has a bandwidth of 4 kHz and a signal-to-noise power ratio of 1023. Its theoretical maximum capacity is
exp: Shannon's formula is $C = B\log_2(1 + S/N)$. Here $1 + S/N = 1024 = 2^{10}$, so $\log_2 1024 = 10$ exactly and $C = 4000 \times 10 = \mathbf{40\ \text{kbps}}$. The value 80 kbps comes from wrongly inserting Nyquist's factor of 2 into Shannon's formula.
trick: Exam setters choose $S/N$ so that $1+S/N$ is a power of 2. Add 1 first and look for $2^k$ — the logarithm is then exact and no calculator is needed.

q: A noiseless channel of bandwidth 8 kHz is to carry 64 kbps. The number of signal levels required is
exp: For a noiseless channel Nyquist gives $C = 2B\log_2 L$. Substituting, $64000 = 2 \times 8000 \times \log_2 L$, so $\log_2 L = 64000/16000 = 4$ and $L = 2^4 = \mathbf{16}$ levels.
trick: Nyquist has the factor 2 (one signal element per half cycle); Shannon does not. If the stem mentions noise or an SNR, there is no 2.

q: A channel of bandwidth 1 MHz has a signal-to-noise ratio of 63. If a system is to operate at the Shannon capacity of this channel over a noiseless equivalent, how many signal levels does Nyquist say are needed?
exp: First apply Shannon: $C = 10^{6} \times \log_2(1+63) = 10^{6} \times \log_2 64 = 6 \times 10^{6}$ bps. Now set Nyquist equal to that rate: $6 \times 10^{6} = 2 \times 10^{6} \times \log_2 L$, so $\log_2 L = 3$ and $L = \mathbf{8}$. The distractor 64 is the value of $1 + S/N$, not the number of levels.
trick: Shannon fixes the rate, Nyquist converts that rate into levels. Doing them in the other order gives nonsense, because Nyquist alone has no upper bound.

q: A 1000-byte packet is sent on a 1 Mbps link that is 2500 km long. The propagation speed is $2.5 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. The total of the transmission delay and the propagation delay is
exp: Transmission delay is $L/R = (1000 \times 8)/10^{6} = 8000/10^{6} = 8$ ms. Propagation delay is $d/v = (2.5 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m})/(2.5 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}) = 10^{-2}$ s $= 10$ ms. Their sum is $\mathbf{18\ \text{ms}}$.
trick: Transmission delay depends on packet size and link rate only; propagation delay depends on distance and speed only. Doubling the link length changes one term and not the other.

q: A 100 Mbps link is 1000 km long and the signal propagates at $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. The number of bits 'in flight' on the link at any instant (its bandwidth-delay product) is
exp: The one-way propagation delay is $d/v = 10^{6}/(2 \times 10^{8}) = 5 \times 10^{-3}$ s $= 5$ ms. The bandwidth-delay product is then $10^{8} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = \mathbf{5 \times 10^{5}}$ bits. That is the number of bits the sender can push out before the first one arrives, and hence the minimum window a sliding-window protocol needs to keep the link busy in one direction.
trick: Bandwidth-delay product $=$ rate $\times$ propagation delay. It reappears as the sliding-window size in 9.5 and as the minimum Ethernet frame size in 9.6, so computing it is never wasted work.

q: Which statement about transmission modes is correct?
opts: Simplex allows transmission in both directions but not simultaneously
Full duplex requires two separate physical media in every implementation
In half duplex the transmitting station gets the whole channel capacity during its turn
In half duplex each station gets half the channel capacity during its turn
exp: Half duplex means only one side transmits at a time, so whichever side holds the channel has **all** of it — that is (B), and (A) inverts it. Simplex is one-directional only, so (C) actually describes half duplex. Full duplex can be realised either with two physical paths or by splitting one channel's capacity between the directions, so (D) is too strong.
trick: Examiners phrase full duplex as 'capacity is divided between the two directions' and half duplex as 'the entire capacity is available to the transmitting station'. Learn those two phrasings.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (switching technique) | List-II (property) |
|---|---|
| (a) Circuit switching | (i) each packet carries a full destination address and is routed independently |
| (b) Datagram packet switching | (ii) a setup phase reserves a dedicated path, which stays idle when nobody speaks |
| (c) Virtual-circuit packet switching | (iii) the entire message is stored and forwarded at each node with no size limit |
| (d) Message switching | (iv) a path is set up once, after which packets carry only a short identifier |
exp: Circuit switching reserves a physical path in a setup phase and holds it even during silence, which is (ii). A datagram network has no setup, so each packet must carry the full address and may take its own route — (i). A virtual circuit is set up once and packets then carry only a short VC identifier, arriving in order — (iv). Message switching stores whole messages at every hop with no maximum size, which is why it died for interactive traffic — (iii).
trick: Ask two questions: is there a setup phase, and does every packet carry a full address? Yes/no gives circuit, no/yes gives datagram, yes/no-short-id gives virtual circuit.

q: An analog signal band-limited to 5 kHz is digitised by PCM with 1024 quantisation levels. The resulting bit rate is
exp: The Nyquist sampling rate is $f_s = 2 f_{\max} = 2 \times 5000 = 10\,000$ samples/s. With 1024 levels each sample needs $\log_2 1024 = 10$ bits. The bit rate is therefore $N = f_s \times n = 10\,000 \times 10 = \mathbf{100\ \text{kbps}}$.
trick: Two steps, always: $f_s = 2f_{\max}$, then $n = \log_2 L$, then multiply. Note $f_{\max}$, not the bandwidth — for a 300–3400 Hz signal the sampling rate is 6800 Hz, not 6200 Hz.

q: A bit stream is transmitted at 100 Mbps using Manchester encoding. The signal (baud) rate is
exp: Manchester encoding puts a transition in the middle of every bit, so each bit occupies **two** signal elements and $r = 1/2$ bits per signal element. Since $S = N/r$, the signal rate is $100/(1/2) = \mathbf{200\ \text{Mbaud}}$ — double the bit rate. That doubled bandwidth requirement is exactly the price paid for guaranteed clock recovery.
trick: Write $S = N/r$ and remember $r$: NRZ and AMI have $r = 1$; Manchester, differential Manchester and RZ have $r = 1/2$; 4B/5B has $r = 4/5$ (so 100 Mbps runs at 125 Mbaud); $M$-ary modulation has $r = \log_2 M$.

q: A modem transmits 12 kbps using 3000 signal elements per second. The modulation scheme in use is
exp: Bits per symbol is $r = N/S = 12000/3000 = 4$, so the constellation has $2^4 = 16$ points. Among the options, only **16-QAM** carries 4 bits per symbol; QPSK carries 2, 8-PSK carries 3 and 64-QAM carries 6.
trick: $M = 2^{N/S}$. The four values worth memorising are BPSK 1, QPSK 2, 8-PSK 3, 16-QAM 4, 64-QAM 6, 256-QAM 8 bits per symbol.

q: In the T1 carrier, 24 voice channels are combined by synchronous TDM. Each channel is sampled 8000 times per second at 8 bits per sample and one framing bit is added per frame. The line rate is
exp: Each frame carries one 8-bit sample from each of the 24 channels plus 1 framing bit, i.e. $24 \times 8 + 1 = 193$ bits. A frame is needed for every sampling instant, so frames occur 8000 times per second. The line rate is $193 \times 8000 = 1\,544\,000$ bps $= \mathbf{1.544\ \text{Mbps}}$. The distractor 1.536 Mbps is $24 \times 64$ kbps, the payload without the framing bit.
trick: Four numbers answer most multiplexing questions: one digital voice channel is 64 kbps, T1 is 1.544 Mbps with 24 channels, E1 is 2.048 Mbps with 32 slots of which 30 carry voice.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes synchronous TDM from statistical TDM?
opts: In synchronous TDM each slot carries an address; in statistical TDM it does not
Synchronous TDM is used in analog systems and statistical TDM in digital systems
Statistical TDM wastes a slot whenever an input has nothing to send
In statistical TDM the output rate can be less than the sum of the input rates, because slots are given only to active inputs
exp: Synchronous TDM gives every input a fixed slot in every frame whether or not it has data, so empty slots are transmitted and the output rate must equal the sum of the input rates plus framing. Statistical TDM allocates slots on demand, so the link can be dimensioned below the sum of the inputs — which is (B) and makes (D) a description of synchronous TDM. Because a slot no longer implies a source, statistical TDM must add an **address** to each slot, so (A) is reversed. Both are digital, so (C) is wrong; frequency-division multiplexing is the analog one.
trick: Guard band goes with FDM (frequency), framing bit goes with synchronous TDM (time), per-slot address goes with statistical TDM. Each keyword names one scheme.

q: Data $1011001$ is to be transmitted with a CRC generated by the polynomial $x^3 + x^2 + 1$ (bit pattern $1101$). The transmitted frame is
exp: The generator has degree $r = 3$, so 3 zeros are appended, giving the dividend $1011001\,000$, and the CRC will be 3 bits long. Dividing by $1101$ with XOR in place of subtraction leaves the remainder $\mathbf{110}$. The transmitted frame is the data followed by that remainder, $1011001\,\mathbf{110}$. Checking, dividing $1011001110$ by $1101$ gives remainder $000$, so the receiver accepts it.
trick: The CRC length is always the degree of the generator, i.e. one less than the number of bits in the generator string — no division needed to answer 'how many redundant bits'.

q: A CRC uses the generator $11001$. Which of the following is guaranteed about its error-detection capability?
opts: It detects all burst errors of length 5 or less
It detects all burst errors of length 4 or less
It detects all burst errors of length 8 or less
exp: The generator $11001$ has 5 bits and hence degree $r = 4$. A CRC with a degree-$r$ generator is guaranteed to detect every burst error whose length is at most $r$, so **all bursts of length 4 or less** are caught. Bursts of exactly $r+1 = 5$ bits escape with probability $(1/2)^{r-1}$ and longer bursts with probability $(1/2)^{r}$, so (A) overstates it. CRC is a detection code only; it does not correct, so (D) is false.
trick: The single number $r$ (the generator's degree) fixes the CRC length, the number of appended zeros and the guaranteed burst length. Read it off the generator and every part of the question is answered.

q: How many check bits does a Hamming single-error-correcting code need for 16 data bits, and what is the total codeword length?
exp: The condition is $2^{r} \ge m + r + 1$ with $m = 16$. Trying $r = 4$: $2^{4} = 16$ but $m + r + 1 = 21$, and $16 < 21$, so 4 is not enough. Trying $r = 5$: $2^{5} = 32 \ge 16 + 5 + 1 = 22$, which holds. So $r = \mathbf{5}$ and the codeword is $16 + 5 = \mathbf{21}$ bits.
trick: Test $r$ upward from $\lceil \log_2 m \rceil$; the first value satisfying $2^r \ge m+r+1$ wins. The ladder is: 4 data bits need 3 checks, 8 or 11 need 4, 12 to 26 need 5, 27 to 57 need 6.

q: A 7-bit Hamming codeword with even parity is received. Parity checks $C_1$ (positions 1,3,5,7) and $C_4$ (positions 4,5,6,7) fail, while $C_2$ (positions 2,3,6,7) passes. The erroneous bit is at position
exp: The syndrome is formed by writing the check results as a binary number with $C_1$ as the least significant bit: $C_4 C_2 C_1 = 1\,0\,1$. Read as binary, $101_2 = \mathbf{5}$, so bit 5 is the corrupted one. The construction guarantees this, because position 5 is $101$ in binary and is therefore covered by exactly checks $C_1$ and $C_4$ and by no other.
trick: The failing checks written as a binary number *are* the error position in decimal, with $p_1$ as the least significant bit. A syndrome of 0 means no single-bit error.

q: A block code has a minimum Hamming distance of 6. The number of errors it can detect and the number it can correct are respectively
exp: Detection requires $d_{\min} \ge s+1$, so $s = d_{\min} - 1 = \mathbf{5}$ errors can be detected. Correction requires $d_{\min} \ge 2t+1$, so $t = \lfloor (d_{\min}-1)/2 \rfloor = \lfloor 5/2 \rfloor = \mathbf{2}$ errors can be corrected. Note the two capabilities are alternatives, not simultaneous: a receiver configured to correct 2 errors will mis-handle a genuine 5-error pattern.
trick: Detect $= d-1$; correct $= \lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor$. For $d = 3$ that is 2 and 1; for $d = 4$, 3 and 1; for $d = 5$, 4 and 2; for $d = 6$, 5 and 2.

q:
Consider the following statements.

(A) A simple parity bit detects every error pattern involving an odd number of bits.
(B) A simple parity bit can locate the position of a single-bit error.
(C) Two-dimensional parity can correct a single-bit error.
(D) The Internet checksum is computed using one's complement addition with an end-around carry.

Which statements are correct?
exp: (A) is correct — an odd number of flips always changes the parity, while an even number restores it, which is why parity misses all even-numbered error patterns. (B) is false: one bit of redundancy carries only a yes/no verdict and cannot name a position. (C) is correct because a failing row and a failing column intersect at exactly one cell. (D) is correct: the sender adds the words in one's complement, wrapping any carry out of the top bit back into the bottom, then complements the sum.
trick: Locating an error needs enough syndrome values to name every position, which is why Hamming needs $2^r \ge m+r+1$. One parity bit gives two syndromes and can therefore only say 'good' or 'bad'.

q: A burst error of length 8 in a received frame means that
opts: the first and the last corrupted bits are 8 positions apart, with some bits in between possibly unchanged
8 consecutive bits have all been inverted
8 separate bursts have occurred in the frame
exp: Burst length is measured as a **span**, from the first corrupted bit to the last, inclusive — the bits inside the span may or may not have been flipped. So a length-8 burst involves at most 8 flipped bits but possibly as few as 2. This matters because CRC guarantees are stated in terms of the span: a degree-$r$ generator detects every burst whose span is at most $r$, regardless of how many bits inside it actually changed.
trick: Whenever a question says 'burst of length $k$', read 'span $k$', not '$k$ flipped bits'. The CRC guarantee is about the span.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (OSI layer) | List-II (function) |
|---|---|
| (a) Data link | (i) translation between data representations, encryption and compression |
| (b) Network | (ii) process-to-process delivery with end-to-end error and flow control |
| (c) Transport | (iii) framing, physical addressing and node-to-node error control |
| (d) Presentation | (iv) logical addressing, routing and fragmentation |
exp: The data link layer frames the bit stream, uses MAC addresses and does hop-by-hop error control: (a)-(iii). The network layer assigns logical (IP) addresses, routes between networks and fragments to fit an MTU: (b)-(iv). The transport layer is the first layer that knows about processes, giving end-to-end delivery with its own error and flow control: (c)-(ii). The presentation layer deals with the syntax of the data — representation translation, encryption and compression: (d)-(i).
trick: 'Node to node' means data link, 'host to host' means network, 'process to process' means transport. The phrase in the stem names the layer.

q: A datagram travels from a source host through two routers to a destination host. Over this journey, how many times do the source MAC address and the source IP address in the frames/packets change?
exp: IP addresses are end-to-end identifiers and are not rewritten by routers (barring NAT), so the source IP stays the same throughout — 0 changes. MAC addresses are link-local: the frame is rebuilt on each of the three links (host to router 1, router 1 to router 2, router 2 to destination), so a different source MAC is written each time, i.e. the field takes **3** different values over the path.
trick: The IP header survives the journey; the frame header is discarded and rebuilt at every hop. That one sentence answers every addressing-across-routers question.

q: Which pair of OSI layers has no separately identified counterpart in the four-layer TCP/IP model?
exp: In the TCP/IP model the physical and data link layers are merged into a single network-access (link) layer, so they are still present, just combined; the network layer becomes the Internet layer and the transport layer keeps its name. The **session** and **presentation** layers have no separate existence at all: dialog control, representation, encryption and compression are handled inside the application itself.
trick: The mapping is Application = OSI 5+6+7, Transport = 4, Internet = 3, Link = 1+2. Only the top three collapse into one, which is why session and presentation vanish.

q: A 10 Mbps link carries 10,000-bit frames and has a one-way propagation delay of 20 ms. Under Stop-and-Wait ARQ, the link utilisation is approximately
exp: Transmission time is $T_t = 10\,000/10^{7} = 1$ ms. The ratio $a = T_p/T_t = 20/1 = 20$. Stop-and-Wait utilisation is $\eta = 1/(1+2a) = 1/41 = 0.0244 = \mathbf{2.44\%}$. The link spends over 97% of its time idle waiting for acknowledgements.
trick: Compute $a = T_p/T_t$ first; then $1/(1+2a)$ for Stop-and-Wait and $W/(1+2a)$ for a window of $W$. If the stem gives RTT instead of $T_p$, the denominator is $1 + \text{RTT}/T_t$.

q: For the same link ($T_t = 1$ ms, one-way propagation delay 20 ms), the minimum sender window size needed for 100% utilisation is
exp: Full utilisation requires the sender to keep transmitting for one whole round trip, so $W \ge 1 + 2a$. With $a = 20$ this gives $W \ge 1 + 40 = \mathbf{41}$ frames. The 1 accounts for the frame currently being transmitted and the $2a$ for the frames that could be sent during the round-trip propagation.
trick: $W = 1 + 2a$, and remember the $+1$: 40 (the pure bandwidth-delay term) is always offered as a distractor.

q: Still on the same link ($1+2a = 41$), what is the minimum number of sequence-number bits required under Go-Back-N and under Selective Repeat respectively, so that a window of 41 frames can be used?
exp: Go-Back-N permits a sender window of at most $2^{m}-1$, so $2^{m} - 1 \ge 41$ needs $2^{m} \ge 42$; since $2^{5} = 32 < 42$ and $2^{6} = 64 \ge 42$, $m = \mathbf{6}$ bits. Selective Repeat permits at most $2^{m-1}$, so $2^{m-1} \ge 41$ needs $m-1 = 6$ (as $2^{5} = 32 < 41$), giving $m = \mathbf{7}$ bits. Selective Repeat costs one extra sequence bit because the receiver window must also fit in the sequence space.
trick: Go-Back-N: $2^m - 1$. Selective Repeat: $2^{m-1}$. With 3 bits that is 7 and 4; with 4 bits, 15 and 8; with 5 bits, 31 and 16.

q: A protocol uses a 5-bit sequence number field. The maximum sender window sizes permitted under Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat are
exp: With $m = 5$ there are $2^{5} = 32$ distinct sequence numbers. Go-Back-N allows $2^{m} - 1 = \mathbf{31}$: a full window of 32 would let a retransmitted old frame be mistaken for a new one after a lost acknowledgement. Selective Repeat allows only $2^{m-1} = \mathbf{16}$, because the sender and receiver windows can both be open simultaneously and together must not exceed the sequence space.
trick: 'Minus one for Go-Back-N, half for Selective Repeat.' Also note that 'how many sequence numbers are needed for a window of $W$' is a different question from 'what is the maximum window'.

q: Under Go-Back-N with a window of 6, the sender has transmitted frames 0 through 5 when frame 2 is lost. Assuming no further losses, how many frames in total does the sender retransmit?
exp: The receiver discards everything after the gap, so frames 3, 4 and 5 are thrown away even though they arrived intact. On the timeout for frame 2 the sender goes back to it and resends frame 2 and everything after it that was outstanding: frames 2, 3, 4 and 5 — **4 frames**. Under Selective Repeat only frame 2 would be resent, which is the distractor 1.
trick: Go-Back-N retransmits the lost frame plus every frame sent after it, which is at most $W$ frames. Selective Repeat always retransmits exactly 1.

q: The bit sequence $0111111011111110$ is to be sent inside an HDLC frame using bit stuffing. How many 0 bits are stuffed?
exp: HDLC inserts a 0 after every run of five consecutive 1s so that the flag pattern $01111110$ can never appear in the payload. Scanning the data: the first run is $111111$ — after the fifth 1 a 0 is stuffed. The second run is $1111111$ — again a 0 is stuffed after its fifth 1. No other run reaches five 1s, so exactly **2** zeros are stuffed and the 16-bit input becomes 18 bits on the wire.
trick: Count runs of 1s and take $\lfloor \text{run length}/5 \rfloor$ for each run, remembering that the stuffed 0 breaks the run and the count restarts.

q: Which statement about HDLC frame types is correct?
opts: Only U-frames may carry a poll/final bit
S-frames carry user data together with a piggybacked acknowledgement
U-frames manage the link with commands such as SABM and DISC
I-frames carry only supervisory information such as RR and RNR
exp: I-frames (control field beginning with 0) carry user data plus $N(S)$, $N(R)$ and the poll/final bit, so (A) and (B) have I and S swapped. S-frames (beginning 10) carry supervisory control only — RR, RNR, REJ and SREJ. U-frames (beginning 11) are the link-management frames: SABM to set the mode, UA to acknowledge it, DISC to disconnect and FRMR to report a frame reject. The poll/final bit appears in all three types, so (D) is false.
trick: Decode the control field's first bits: `0` means information, `10` means supervisory, `11` means unnumbered. The bit pattern names the frame type.

q: A CSMA/CD network operates at 10 Mbps over a 2 km cable with a signal propagation speed of $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. The minimum frame size required for collision detection to work is
exp: The one-way propagation time is $\tau = 2000/(2 \times 10^{8}) = 10^{-5}$ s $= 10\ \mu$s, so the round-trip worst case is $2\tau = 20\ \mu$s. A station must still be transmitting when the collision fragment gets back, so $L_{\min} = 2\tau \times R = 20 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{7} = \mathbf{200}$ bits. The option 512 bits is the value for standard Ethernet, whose slot time is 51.2 µs, not 20 µs.
trick: $L_{\min} = 2 \times R \times \tau$ — twice the bandwidth-delay product. Every variant of this question is that one line rearranged for whichever quantity is missing.

q: Standard Ethernet fixes the minimum frame at 512 bits. If the data rate is raised from 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps while keeping that minimum, the maximum network span
exp: From $L_{\min} = 2R\tau$ we get $\tau = L_{\min}/(2R)$, and the span is $d = v\tau$, so with $L_{\min}$ fixed the span is inversely proportional to $R$. Multiplying the rate by 100 therefore divides the span by **100** — from about 2.5 km down to tens of metres. This is precisely why Gigabit Ethernet introduced carrier extension (padding the slot time to 512 bytes) and, in practice, abandoned CSMA/CD for full-duplex switching.
trick: $d \propto L_{\min}/(2R)$. Faster link, shorter cable — unless the minimum frame size is increased in step.

q: A pure ALOHA network transmits 200-bit frames on a 200 kbps channel. If the system as a whole produces 1000 frames per second, the number of frames that are transmitted successfully per second is approximately
exp: The frame time is $T_{fr} = 200/200\,000 = 1$ ms, so the offered load in frames per frame-time is $G = 1000 \times 0.001 = 1$. Pure ALOHA throughput is $S = Ge^{-2G} = 1 \times e^{-2} = 0.135$ frames per frame-time. Multiplying by the 1000 frame-times per second gives about **135** successful frames per second. Note that 184 is the *maximum* pure-ALOHA throughput, reached at $G = 0.5$, not the value at $G = 1$.
trick: Pure ALOHA $S = Ge^{-2G}$ (peak $1/2e = 0.184$ at $G = 0.5$); slotted ALOHA $S = Ge^{-G}$ (peak $1/e = 0.368$ at $G = 1$). Substitute the given $G$ rather than quoting the peak.

q: The minimum and maximum sizes of an IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frame, excluding the preamble and start frame delimiter, are
exp: Add up the fields: destination MAC 6 + source MAC 6 + length/type 2 + data 46 to 1500 + FCS 4. The minimum is $6+6+2+46+4 = \mathbf{64}$ bytes and the maximum is $6+6+2+1500+4 = \mathbf{1518}$ bytes. The pair 46/1500 is the *data field* range, and 72/1526 is what you get by wrongly including the 7-byte preamble and 1-byte SFD, which belong to the physical layer.
trick: 64 and 1518 without the preamble; 72 and 1526 with it; 1522 with an 802.1Q VLAN tag. Read the stem for which extras are included.

q: In Ethernet's binary exponential backoff, after the fourth successive collision on the same frame the station waits $k$ slot times, where $k$ is chosen uniformly at random from
exp: After the $n$-th collision the station picks $k$ uniformly from $\{0, 1, \ldots, 2^{n}-1\}$. With $n = 4$ that set is $\{0, \ldots, 2^{4}-1\} = \{0, \ldots, \mathbf{15}\}$, i.e. 16 possible values including zero. The exponent is capped at 10 (so the range never exceeds 0 to 1023) and the frame is abandoned after 16 attempts.
trick: The range is $0$ to $2^{n}-1$ after the $n$-th collision — always starting at 0, and always $2^n$ possible values.

q: Five hosts are connected to a hub, the hub is connected to one port of an 8-port switch, and the switch is connected to a router. How many collision domains and broadcast domains exist on the switch side of the router?
exp: A hub does not separate anything, so its five hosts plus the link to the switch form a single collision domain — but that is the collision domain belonging to the switch port the hub is attached to. Each of the switch's 8 ports is its own collision domain, giving **8** in total. A switch forwards broadcasts out of every port, so all of them lie in one broadcast domain; only the router's interface breaks that, so there is **1** broadcast domain on this side.
trick: Each switch or bridge port cuts a collision domain; each router interface cuts a broadcast domain; hubs and repeaters cut nothing. Walk the topology and count the pieces.

q: Wireless LANs use CSMA/CA rather than CSMA/CD principally because
opts: a station cannot listen for collisions while transmitting, since its own signal swamps the receiver
collisions never occur in a wireless medium
radio frames are too short for collision detection to be useful
CSMA/CA gives higher throughput than CSMA/CD on every medium
exp: Collision *detection* requires a station to compare what it hears with what it is sending, which a half-duplex radio cannot do — the transmitted signal is many orders of magnitude stronger at its own antenna than any distant station's. Collisions certainly do occur, and the hidden-terminal problem makes them worse, so (C) is false. CSMA/CA therefore *avoids* collisions with interframe spaces, a frozen-countdown backoff, explicit acknowledgements and optional RTS/CTS — mechanisms that cost throughput rather than gain it, so (D) is false too.
trick: Any stem mentioning hidden terminals, RTS/CTS or a network allocation vector is a CSMA/CA question, whatever else appears in the options.

q: A host has the address 192.168.20.130 with mask 255.255.255.192. Its network address and directed broadcast address are
exp: The mask 255.255.255.192 is a /26, and the interesting octet is 192, so the block size is $256 - 192 = 64$. Subnet boundaries in the last octet are therefore 0, 64, 128 and 192. The host octet 130 falls in the block starting at 128, so the network address is **192.168.20.128** and the broadcast address is one below the next boundary, **192.168.20.191**. The usable host range is .129 to .190, which is $2^{6}-2 = 62$ addresses.
trick: Block size $= 256 -$ the interesting mask octet. Round the host's octet down to the nearest multiple of the block size for the network address, and add block size $-1$ for the broadcast.

q: The network 200.10.5.0/24 is to be divided into subnets each supporting at least 30 hosts. The correct prefix, the number of such subnets, and the usable hosts per subnet are
exp: Thirty usable hosts requires $2^{h} - 2 \ge 30$, so $2^{h} \ge 32$ and $h = 5$ host bits, giving a prefix of $32 - 5 = /27$. Borrowing $27 - 24 = 3$ bits from the /24 yields $2^{3} = \mathbf{8}$ subnets, each with $2^{5} - 2 = \mathbf{30}$ usable hosts. A /28 would give only 14 hosts, too few, and a /26 wastes half the space.
trick: Learn the host ladder: /30 gives 2, /29 gives 6, /28 gives 14, /27 gives 30, /26 gives 62, /25 gives 126, /24 gives 254. A requirement reads straight off it.

q: For the host address 10.20.77.45/18, the network address and the number of usable host addresses are
exp: A /18 mask is 255.255.192.0, so the interesting octet is the third one with value 192 and the block size there is $256 - 192 = 64$. Third-octet boundaries are 0, 64, 128 and 192; since $77$ lies between 64 and 127, the network address is **10.20.64.0** (broadcast 10.20.127.255). The host part is $32 - 18 = 14$ bits, giving $2^{14} - 2 = \mathbf{16\,382}$ usable addresses.
trick: When the prefix is not a multiple of 8, find the interesting octet first, then apply the 256-minus rule in that octet only. The octets to its left are copied and those to its right are zero.

q: The four networks 192.168.8.0/24, 192.168.9.0/24, 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.11.0/24 are aggregated into a single route. The resulting supernet is
exp: Combining $4 = 2^{2}$ consecutive /24 blocks means shortening the prefix by 2 bits, giving a /22. The aggregation is legal only if the first block's third octet is divisible by 4, and $8 \bmod 4 = 0$, so it is. The supernet is **192.168.8.0/22** with mask 255.255.252.0, covering the third octets 8, 9, 10 and 11 — a total of 1024 addresses.
trick: To aggregate $2^{k}$ consecutive blocks, check that the first block number is divisible by $2^{k}$, then subtract $k$ from the prefix length. 8, 9, 10, 11 works; 9, 10, 11, 12 does not.

q: How many /28 subnets can be carved out of the block 172.20.0.0/22?
exp: Going from a /22 to a /28 borrows $28 - 22 = 6$ bits, so the number of subnets is $2^{6} = \mathbf{64}$. Checking by address count: a /22 contains $2^{10} = 1024$ addresses and a /28 contains $2^{4} = 16$, and $1024/16 = 64$.
trick: Number of subnets $= 2^{(\text{new prefix} - \text{old prefix})}$. Verifying it by dividing the two block sizes catches arithmetic slips.

q: A 5000-byte IPv4 datagram (including a 20-byte header) must cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes. Assuming no options, how many fragments are produced and what is the fragment offset field of the last fragment?
exp: The payload is $5000 - 20 = 4980$ bytes. Each fragment may carry at most $1500 - 20 = 1480$ bytes, and 1480 is a multiple of 8 so no rounding down is needed. Three fragments carry 1480 bytes each ($3 \times 1480 = 4440$) and a fourth carries the remaining $4980 - 4440 = 540$ bytes — **4 fragments**. The offset is measured in 8-byte units, so the last fragment begins at byte 4440 and its offset field holds $4440/8 = \mathbf{555}$.
trick: Fragment offset is in units of 8 bytes, so divide the byte position by 8. Every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes, which is why the payload is 1480 and never 1479 or 1481.

q: In the IPv4 header, the HLEN field contains the value 5 and the total length field contains 1500. The number of bytes of payload carried by this datagram is
exp: HLEN counts the header length in **4-byte words**, so a value of 5 means a header of $5 \times 4 = 20$ bytes. Total length counts the header plus the data in **bytes**, so the payload is $1500 - 20 = \mathbf{1480}$ bytes. Mixing these two units is the single most common error in this topic; the maximum HLEN value of 15 corresponds to a 60-byte header.
trick: Three fields, three units: HLEN in 4-byte words, total length in bytes, fragment offset in 8-byte units. Write the unit beside each number before computing.

q: Which IPv4 header field has no counterpart in the IPv6 base header?
exp: IPv6 deliberately drops the **header checksum**: the data link layer already detects errors and the transport layer has a mandatory checksum of its own, so recomputing a header checksum at every router was pure cost. TTL survives under the name hop limit, the addresses survive at 128 bits each, and the version field is still there holding 6. IPv6 also removes the header length field (the base header is a fixed 40 bytes), the fragmentation fields and the options area.
trick: IPv6 removed four things: header checksum, header length, fragmentation fields and in-header options. A question asking what IPv4 has and IPv6 does not is usually after the checksum.

q: An organisation with the block 200.15.20.0/24 must serve two LANs of 50 hosts each, one LAN of 30 hosts and two point-to-point links of 2 hosts each, using VLSM. What is the total number of addresses consumed?
exp: Allocate largest first. Each 50-host LAN needs $2^{h}-2 \ge 50$, so $h = 6$ and the prefix is /26, consuming 64 addresses each: $2 \times 64 = 128$. The 30-host LAN needs $2^{5}-2 = 30$ exactly, so /27, consuming 32. Each point-to-point link needs $2^{2}-2 = 2$, so /30, consuming 4 each: $2 \times 4 = 8$. The total is $128 + 32 + 8 = \mathbf{196}$ addresses, leaving 60 free at the top of the block.
trick: Always allocate the largest requirement first. Every block must begin at a multiple of its own size, so placing a /30 in the middle of the space can make a later /26 unplaceable.

q: Which statement about ARP is correct?
opts: ARP resolves an IP address into a MAC address; the request is broadcast and the reply is unicast
ARP requests and replies are both broadcast, and results are never cached
ARP resolves a MAC address into an IP address and is carried inside an IP datagram
ARP is used only when the destination lies on a different network
exp: ARP answers the question 'which MAC address owns this IP address?'. The requester broadcasts the query so that every station on the link sees it, and only the owner replies — unicast, since the reply can use the requester's MAC address taken from the request. The result is cached with a timeout, which is what keeps ARP traffic negligible. (A) describes RARP and also gets the encapsulation wrong: ARP rides directly in an Ethernet frame with type 0x0806, not inside IP. (D) is backwards — for an off-link destination ARP is used to find the *router's* MAC address.
trick: Request broadcast, reply unicast, result cached. Reversing the request/reply direction gives RARP, which DHCP has replaced.

q: In the weighted graph with edges A–B = 2, A–C = 5, B–C = 1, B–D = 7, C–D = 3, C–E = 8 and D–E = 2, the shortest-path distances from A to D and to E, computed by Dijkstra's algorithm, are
exp: Start with A = 0. Relaxing A's edges gives B = 2 and C = 5. Finalise B (2) and relax: C via B is $2+1 = 3 < 5$, so C = 3; D via B is $2+7 = 9$. Finalise C (3) and relax: D via C is $3+3 = 6 < 9$, so **D = 6**; E via C is $3+8 = 11$. Finalise D (6) and relax: E via D is $6+2 = 8 < 11$, so **E = 8**. Finalise E (8). The paths are A–B–C–D and A–B–C–D–E.
trick: Never assume a direct edge is the shortest path — here A–C costs 5 but A–B–C costs only 3. Finalise the smallest tentative node, relax only its edges, repeat exactly $n$ times.

q: Router X has two neighbours: Y over a link of cost 2 and Z over a link of cost 7. X currently records destination D at cost 8 via Z. It now receives distance vectors saying Y reaches D at cost 3 and Z reaches D at cost 1. After the Bellman–Ford update, X's entry for D is
exp: Bellman–Ford evaluates $c(X,v) + D_v(D)$ for every neighbour $v$ and takes the minimum. Via Y the cost is $2 + 3 = 5$; via Z it is $7 + 1 = 8$. The minimum is 5, so X installs **cost 5 with next hop Y**, replacing the old cost-8 entry. Options 3 and 1 are the neighbours' advertised costs without adding the link cost.
trick: Tabulate link cost plus advertised cost for each neighbour on one line and pick the minimum. Forgetting to add the link cost to the neighbour is the standard error.

q: Split horizon with poison reverse in a distance-vector protocol prevents
opts: the flooding of link state advertisements
exp: Poison reverse advertises a route back out of the interface it was learned on, but with a metric of infinity, so the upstream neighbour can never believe it has an alternative path through the downstream one. That kills the two-router count-to-infinity cycle. Loops involving three or more routers can still form, because each router only suppresses the single neighbour it learned the route from — which is why RIP additionally needs hold-down timers, triggered updates and a finite infinity of 16.
trick: Split horizon and poison reverse fix the two-node loop only. Any option offering 'all routing loops' overstates them.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (protocol) | List-II (characteristic) |
|---|---|
| (a) RIP | (i) path vector, runs over TCP port 179, detects loops by inspecting the AS path |
| (b) OSPF | (ii) distance vector, hop-count metric, infinity = 16, updates every 30 s |
| (c) BGP | (iii) link state, floods LSAs within an area, runs directly over IP protocol 89 |
| (d) Dijkstra's algorithm | (iv) computes a shortest-path tree from a complete topology map |
exp: RIP is the classic distance-vector IGP with a hop-count metric, a maximum of 15 usable hops and 16 meaning unreachable, sending its table every 30 seconds: (a)-(ii). OSPF is the link-state IGP that floods link-state advertisements inside an area and runs directly over IP as protocol 89: (b)-(iii). BGP is the inter-domain path-vector protocol over TCP 179, rejecting any route whose AS path already contains its own AS number: (c)-(i). Dijkstra is the algorithm each link-state router runs on its own copy of the topology: (d)-(iv).
trick: Identify the family from what is exchanged: whole table to neighbours = distance vector; own link states to everybody = link state; full AS sequence = path vector.

q: Which statement about OSPF is FALSE?
opts: It supports load balancing across multiple equal-cost paths
It floods link state advertisements to every router within an area
It periodically sends its complete routing table to its directly connected neighbours
Its default metric is derived from interface bandwidth, not hop count
exp: Sending the whole routing table to neighbours periodically is **distance-vector** behaviour and belongs to RIP; OSPF never does it. What OSPF floods is small link-state advertisements describing a router's own links, and it does so on change plus a slow refresh, so every router builds an identical topology database and runs Dijkstra on it. The remaining three statements are all true of OSPF.
trick: Cost from bandwidth means OSPF; cost from hop count means RIP. A two-hop gigabit path beats a one-hop 64 kbps path in OSPF, which is impossible in RIP.

q: A TCP Reno connection has MSS = 1 KB. When the congestion window reaches 64 KB a timeout occurs. How many round-trip times pass before the congestion window again reaches 64 KB?
exp: On a timeout, ssthresh becomes $\text{cwnd}/2 = 32$ KB and cwnd is reset to 1 KB, restarting slow start. Slow start doubles cwnd each RTT: after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 RTTs it is 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 KB — **5 RTTs** to reach ssthresh. TCP then enters congestion avoidance, adding 1 MSS per RTT, so climbing from 32 KB to 64 KB takes a further $64 - 32 = 32$ RTTs. The total is $5 + 32 = \mathbf{37}$ RTTs.
trick: Total $= \log_2(\text{ssthresh}) + (\text{target} - \text{ssthresh})$ RTTs when cwnd restarts at 1 MSS. Here $\log_2 32 = 5$ plus $64-32 = 32$, giving 37 without drawing a table.

q: For the same connection (timeout at cwnd = 64 KB, MSS = 1 KB), what is the congestion window 8 RTTs after the timeout?
exp: After the timeout, ssthresh = 32 KB and cwnd = 1 KB. Slow start gives cwnd = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 KB after RTTs 1 to 5. From RTT 6 onward the connection is in congestion avoidance, adding 1 KB per RTT: 33 KB after RTT 6, 34 KB after RTT 7 and **35 KB** after RTT 8.
trick: Write the table rather than trusting arithmetic — 'after $n$ RTTs' and 'at RTT $n$' differ by one, and that off-by-one is the whole point of these questions.

q: A TCP Reno sender has cwnd = 24 MSS and ssthresh = 30 MSS when three duplicate acknowledgements arrive. Immediately afterwards, ssthresh and cwnd are
exp: Three duplicate ACKs indicate that packets are still reaching the receiver, so Reno treats it as mild congestion: it performs fast retransmit and then fast recovery, setting $\text{ssthresh} = \text{cwnd}/2 = \mathbf{12}$ and $\text{cwnd} = \text{ssthresh} = \mathbf{12}$, continuing in congestion avoidance without a slow-start phase. Both halvings use the *current cwnd*, not the old ssthresh, so 15 is wrong. TCP Tahoe would instead drop cwnd to 1 and restart slow start, giving ssthresh = 12 with cwnd = 1.
trick: Timeout means cwnd goes to 1; three duplicate ACKs in Reno mean cwnd goes to half. Read the stem for which event occurred before touching the arithmetic.

q: A TCP connection has a round-trip time of 20 ms and the receiver advertises a window of 32 KB. Ignoring losses, the maximum achievable throughput is approximately
exp: Throughput is window divided by round-trip time, with the window converted to bits: $32 \times 1024 \times 8 = 262\,144$ bits. Dividing by 0.02 s gives $13\,107\,200$ bps $\approx \mathbf{13.1\ \text{Mbps}}$. The distractor 1.6 Mbps comes from forgetting the factor of 8 and treating the window as bytes per second.
trick: Convert the window to bits first — a 32 KB window is 262,144 bits, not 32,768. Omitting the factor 8 is the commonest slip in this topic.

q: A client opens a TCP connection with initial sequence number 1000; the server replies with initial sequence number 5000. After the handshake completes, the client sends a segment carrying 200 bytes of data. The sequence number of that data segment and the acknowledgement the server returns are
exp: The SYN itself consumes one sequence number, so after the handshake the client's next byte is numbered $1000 + 1 = 1001$. The data segment therefore carries **seq = 1001** and holds bytes 1001 through 1200. TCP acknowledges the *next expected byte* cumulatively, so the server replies with **ack = 1201**.
trick: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number even though they carry no data, and the acknowledgement names the next byte expected, not the last byte received. Those two rules settle every handshake numbering question.

q: A UDP datagram carries 992 bytes of application data. The values placed in the UDP length field and in the IPv4 total length field (with a 20-byte IP header and no options) are
exp: The UDP length field counts the 8-byte UDP header **plus** the data, so it reads $992 + 8 = \mathbf{1000}$. The IPv4 total length field counts the IP header plus everything it carries, so it reads $20 + 1000 = \mathbf{1020}$. The minimum possible value of the UDP length field is therefore 8, corresponding to an empty datagram.
trick: Chain the three numbers outward: data, then $+8$ for UDP, then $+20$ for IP. Each field includes its own header — a rule IPv6's payload length deliberately breaks.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
opts: Well-known port numbers occupy the range 1024 to 49151
A TCP connection is identified by the four-tuple of source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port
A TCP connection is identified by the destination port alone, which is why a server needs one port per client
TCP connection release requires three segments, like connection establishment
exp: TCP demultiplexes on the full four-tuple, which is exactly why thousands of clients can all talk to one server on port 80 — each connection differs in the client's IP or port. Well-known ports are 0 to 1023; 1024 to 49151 are the registered range, so (C) is wrong. Release needs **four** segments (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK) because each direction closes independently and the passive side may still have data to send, so (D) is wrong.
trick: Setup is three segments because the server combines its SYN and ACK; release is four because there is nothing to combine. Any option offering a three-way termination is wrong.

q: Which statement about SCTP is correct?
opts: SCTP uses a three-way handshake identical to TCP's and is therefore vulnerable to SYN flooding
SCTP provides a half-close facility exactly as TCP does
SCTP supports multihoming and multistreaming, and preserves message boundaries
SCTP is a byte-stream protocol like TCP and does not preserve message boundaries
exp: SCTP is **message oriented**, so it preserves the boundaries of each message the way UDP does, which makes (A) false. Its two headline features are multihoming (an association may bind several IP addresses per endpoint, so a path failure need not kill it) and multistreaming (several independent streams inside one association, so a loss in one does not block the others — no head-of-line blocking). Association setup is a **four-way handshake with a cookie**, which makes it immune to SYN flooding, so (C) is false, and SCTP has no half-close, so (D) is false.
trick: Three facts separate SCTP from TCP: message oriented, multihomed and multistreamed, with a four-way cookie handshake. 'SCTP is a byte stream like TCP' is the standard planted falsehood.

q: A web page consists of a base HTML file and 5 small embedded objects. The round-trip time is 50 ms and all transmission times are negligible. The total retrieval time under non-persistent HTTP with serial connections, and under persistent HTTP with pipelining, are respectively
exp: Non-persistent HTTP opens a fresh TCP connection for every object, costing 1 RTT for the handshake and 1 RTT for the request and response, i.e. 2 RTT per object. With $1 + 5 = 6$ objects that is $12$ RTT $= 12 \times 50 = \mathbf{600\ \text{ms}}$. Persistent HTTP with pipelining costs 1 RTT for the single handshake, 1 RTT for the base file (which must arrive before the browser knows what else to fetch) and 1 RTT for all 5 objects requested back to back: $3$ RTT $= \mathbf{150\ \text{ms}}$. (Persistent without pipelining would cost $1 + 1 + 5 = 7$ RTT $= 350$ ms, the planted distractor.)
trick: With $n$ embedded objects: non-persistent $= 2(n+1)$ RTT, persistent without pipelining $= n+2$ RTT, persistent with pipelining $= 3$ RTT. Three formulas cover every version of this question.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (DNS record type) | List-II (purpose) |
|---|---|
| (a) CNAME | (i) names the mail server for a domain, with a preference value |
| (b) MX | (ii) maps an address back to a name, for reverse lookup |
| (c) PTR | (iii) defines an alias for another name |
| (d) SOA | (iv) holds the zone's parameters, including the serial number and TTLs |
exp: CNAME stands for canonical name and defines an alias pointing at another name: (a)-(iii). MX identifies mail exchangers for a domain and carries a preference value so that backup servers can be listed: (b)-(i). PTR maps an address to a name through the in-addr.arpa tree, which is the reverse lookup: (c)-(ii). SOA, start of authority, carries the zone's administrative parameters such as the serial number, refresh interval and default TTL: (d)-(iv).
trick: The noun in the stem names the record: 'alias' means CNAME, 'mail server' means MX, 'which server is authoritative' means NS, 'reverse lookup' means PTR, 'zone parameters' means SOA.

q: Which statement about DNS transport is correct?
opts: DNS uses only TCP port 53, because reliability is essential
DNS uses only UDP port 53, because queries must be fast
DNS uses UDP port 53 for queries and TCP port 25 for zone transfers
DNS uses UDP port 53 for ordinary queries and TCP port 53 for zone transfers and large responses
exp: Ordinary name queries are short and are sent over UDP 53, where a lost query is simply retried — far cheaper than a TCP handshake. Zone transfers between a primary and its secondaries carry the whole zone and must be reliable, so they use TCP 53, and any response exceeding 512 bytes also falls back to TCP. Port 25 is SMTP and is unrelated.
trick: DNS is the standard example of a protocol that uses both transports. Any option claiming it is UDP-only or TCP-only is wrong.

q: FTP is unusual among application protocols in that it
opts: uses a single TCP connection on port 21 that carries both commands and data
uses two TCP connections — a control connection on port 21 for the whole session and a data connection on port 20 opened for each transfer
requires a separate connection for every command issued
uses UDP for data and TCP for control
exp: FTP separates signalling from bulk transfer. The control connection on **port 21** is opened at login and stays up for the entire session, carrying commands in NVT ASCII. A **data connection on port 20** is created afresh for each file transfer or directory listing and closed when it ends. In active mode the server initiates the data connection back to the client, which firewalls and NAT dislike — the reason passive mode, where the client opens both, is now the default.
trick: 'Which application protocol uses two TCP connections?' and 'why is FTP awkward through NAT?' both have the same answer: the separate data connection.

q: In RSA, $p = 3$, $q = 11$ and the public exponent is $e = 7$. The private exponent $d$ and the ciphertext for $M = 5$ are
exp: Here $n = 3 \times 11 = 33$ and $\phi(n) = 2 \times 10 = 20$; $\gcd(7,20) = 1$, so $e = 7$ is valid. We need $7d \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$, and $7 \times 3 = 21 = 20 + 1$, so $d = \mathbf{3}$. Encrypting: $C = 5^{7} \bmod 33$. By repeated squaring, $5^{2} = 25$, $5^{4} = 25^{2} = 625 = 18 \times 33 + 31 \equiv 31$, so $5^{7} = 5^{4} \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 5 \equiv 31 \times 25 \times 5$. Now $31 \times 25 = 775 = 23 \times 33 + 16 \equiv 16$, and $16 \times 5 = 80 = 2 \times 33 + 14 \equiv \mathbf{14}$. Check: $14^{3} = 2744 = 83 \times 33 + 5 \equiv 5$, recovering $M$.
trick: To find $d$ for small numbers, scan $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ for $(k\phi + 1)/e$ being an integer — here $21/7 = 3$ on the first try. And always reduce mod $n$ at every squaring step rather than computing the full power.

q: In an organisation of 100 people where every pair must be able to communicate privately, the number of keys required under a symmetric scheme and under a public-key scheme are respectively
exp: A symmetric scheme needs one shared secret per unordered pair, i.e. $\binom{100}{2} = \dfrac{100 \times 99}{2} = \mathbf{4950}$ keys, and each person must store and protect 99 of them. A public-key scheme needs only a key pair per person, $2n = \mathbf{200}$ keys in total, of which each person guards exactly one. The growth rates — $O(n^{2})$ against $O(n)$ — are the real scaling argument for public-key cryptography.
trick: $n(n-1)/2$ for symmetric, $2n$ for asymmetric, and $n$ for a Kerberos-style scheme where each party shares one key with a trusted server. A given key count identifies the architecture.

q: Alice wants to send Bob a message that is both confidential and verifiably from her. She should
opts: encrypt the message with her own public key and sign it with Bob's private key
sign the digest with her private key, then encrypt the result with Bob's public key
encrypt with Bob's private key and sign with her public key
encrypt with Bob's public key only
exp: Confidentiality requires encryption under the **recipient's public** key, because only Bob's private key can reverse it. Authentication and non-repudiation require a transformation with the **sender's private** key, because only Alice can produce it and anyone can verify it with her published key. Both goals therefore need both operations, and the signature is applied to the digest rather than the whole message so that it is fast and of fixed size. Options (A) and (C) are impossible: neither party holds the other's private key.
trick: 'Public key locks, private key unlocks' for secrecy; the reverse for signing. If the question wants both properties, both operations must appear.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
opts: 3DES has the same effective key strength as single DES
DES uses a 64-bit block with a 64-bit effective key and 12 rounds
AES uses a block size equal to its key size, so a 256-bit key implies a 256-bit block
AES uses a 128-bit block with a key of 128, 192 or 256 bits and 10, 12 or 14 rounds respectively
exp: AES always operates on a **128-bit block**, whatever the key length; only the key size and hence the round count vary — 128/10, 192/12, 256/14. That makes (B) false, since the block never changes. DES uses a 64-bit block but a **56-bit** effective key (the other 8 bits are parity) and **16** rounds, so (C) is wrong on two counts. 3DES applies DES three times to reach an effective 112 or 168 bits, so (D) is wrong.
trick: A short list answers a question a year: DES 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds; AES 128-bit block always, 128/192/256-bit key with 10/12/14 rounds; MD5 128-bit digest; SHA-1 160; SHA-256 256.

q: IPSec tunnel mode differs from transport mode in that tunnel mode
opts: encapsulates the entire original IP datagram inside a new IP datagram with a new header
can only be used with IPv6
uses AH while transport mode uses ESP
exp: Transport mode protects the payload and leaves the original IP header in place, which suits host-to-host protection. Tunnel mode wraps the **whole original datagram**, header included, inside a new datagram addressed to the security gateways — which hides the internal addresses and is exactly how site-to-site VPNs work. Both AH (integrity and authentication) and ESP (adding confidentiality) can run in either mode, so (A) is a false pairing, and IPSec works with IPv4 as well as IPv6.
trick: Tunnel mode adds a new outer IP header; transport mode does not. If the question mentions a VPN between two gateways or hiding internal addresses, it is tunnel mode.

q: A cellular operator has 20 MHz of uplink spectrum, carriers 200 kHz wide with 8 TDMA slots each, and uses a cluster size of 4. The number of voice channels available per cell is
exp: The spectrum supports $20 \times 10^{6} / (200 \times 10^{3}) = 100$ carriers. Each carrier is divided into 8 TDMA slots, giving $100 \times 8 = 800$ voice channels in the whole system. A cluster of 4 cells shares the entire spectrum between them, so each cell receives $800/4 = \mathbf{200}$ channels.
trick: Total channels $=$ (spectrum $\div$ carrier width) $\times$ slots per carrier; channels per cell $=$ that total $\div$ cluster size $N$. A smaller $N$ raises capacity but shortens the co-channel reuse distance $D/R = \sqrt{3N}$.

q: Four CDMA stations use the length-4 Walsh codes $C_1 = (+1,+1,+1,+1)$, $C_2 = (+1,-1,+1,-1)$, $C_3 = (+1,+1,-1,-1)$ and $C_4 = (+1,-1,-1,+1)$. The composite signal on the channel is $(-1,\ -1,\ +1,\ -3)$. What did station 4 transmit?
opts: the data cannot be recovered without station 4's power level
exp: Decode by taking the inner product of the composite with station 4's own code and dividing by the code length 4: $\dfrac{(-1)(+1) + (-1)(-1) + (+1)(-1) + (-3)(+1)}{4} = \dfrac{-1 + 1 - 1 - 3}{4} = \dfrac{-4}{4} = -1$. A result of $-1$ means the station sent **bit 0** (a station transmits its code for 1, the negated code for 0, and zeros when silent). The other stations contribute exactly zero because the Walsh codes are orthogonal.
trick: Decoding is one dot product divided by the code length: $+1$ means bit 1, $-1$ means bit 0, $0$ means that station was silent. Never try to unmix the composite algebraically.

q: In Mobile IP, a correspondent host sends a packet to a mobile node that is currently on a foreign network. The packet is
opts: sent directly to the mobile node's care-of address
broadcast on every foreign network until the mobile node responds
routed through the foreign agent of the correspondent host
intercepted by the home agent and tunnelled to the care-of address, where the foreign agent delivers it
exp: Correspondents always use the mobile node's permanent **home address**, since that is the only address they know. The **home agent** on the home network intercepts such packets (using proxy ARP), encapsulates each one inside a new IP datagram addressed to the registered **care-of address**, and the foreign agent decapsulates and delivers it locally. Return traffic goes direct, which produces the well-known **triangular routing** inefficiency that route optimisation and reverse tunnelling address.
trick: Inbound goes correspondent $\to$ home agent $\to$ care-of address; outbound goes direct. That asymmetry is the triangle, and remembering the direction answers most Mobile IP questions.

q: Which statement is correct?
opts: RTS/CTS in 802.11 solves the exposed terminal problem
A Bluetooth piconet supports one master and up to seven active slaves, and uses frequency hopping over 79 channels
GSM supports soft handoff because all its cells use the same frequency
A Bluetooth piconet supports one master and up to eight active slaves
exp: A piconet has one master and up to **seven** active slaves (eight active devices in total, plus up to 255 parked), all hopping in step with the master's clock across 79 1 MHz channels in the 2.4 GHz band at 1600 hops per second. (A) inflates the slave count, the standard distractor. Soft handoff belongs to **CDMA**, where neighbouring cells share one frequency; GSM cells use different frequencies and must break before making, so (C) is wrong. RTS/CTS addresses the **hidden** terminal problem by having the receiver announce the reservation; the exposed terminal problem is over-deferral and is not fixed by it, so (D) is wrong.
trick: Hidden terminal causes a collision at the receiver; exposed terminal causes needless silence. If the stem's outcome is a collision it is hidden, if it is wasted capacity it is exposed.

q: A development team pushes application code to a provider that supplies and patches the operating system, the language runtime and the autoscaling, while the team manages only its code and data. This is
exp: The dividing line between models is the highest layer the *provider* manages. In IaaS the provider stops at the virtual hardware and the consumer installs and patches the OS upward. In **PaaS** the provider manages everything below the consumer's code, including the OS, the runtime and scaling, leaving the consumer with applications and data — exactly the situation described. In SaaS the consumer would be using a finished application rather than building one. 'Private cloud' is a deployment model, not a service model, and answers a different question.
trick: Read off what the consumer manages: OS upward means IaaS, applications and data only means PaaS, settings only means SaaS.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five NIST essential characteristics of cloud computing?
exp: The five essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. **Vendor independence** is not among them — indeed proprietary APIs and egress charges make vendor lock-in one of the standard *concerns* about cloud adoption rather than one of its defining properties.
trick: The shape of every NIST definition question is 5-4-3: five essential characteristics, four deployment models (public, private, community, hybrid) and three service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).

q: MQTT runs over TCP while CoAP runs over UDP. A direct consequence of this difference is that
opts: MQTT has the smaller per-message header of the two
CoAP cannot offer any form of reliability
CoAP can address a group of devices using multicast, which MQTT cannot
MQTT cannot provide any guarantee of delivery
exp: UDP supports multicast and TCP does not, so CoAP can address a whole group of constrained devices in one datagram while MQTT, being connection-based, must send to the broker and let it fan out. MQTT does provide delivery guarantees through its QoS levels 0, 1 and 2, so (A) is false, and CoAP layers its own reliability on UDP with confirmable messages and acknowledgements, so (C) is false. CoAP's 4-byte binary header is smaller than MQTT's minimum of two bytes plus topic, and in any case MQTT's advantage comes from reusing one persistent connection, so (D) is not a consequence of the transport choice.
trick: Naming the transport usually names the protocol: MQTT means TCP, a broker, publish/subscribe on topics and QoS 0/1/2; CoAP means UDP, RESTful methods, confirmable messages and multicast.
